# engine

[arc reference](../index.md) › [Products](../index.md#products) › **Product**

## Why it exists

```tagline
The dispatch office. It takes one job, decides which worker should do it, checks the work that comes
back, and writes down who did it and what it cost.
```

# Start here

## In plain words

Think of arc as a small company whose staff are AI models. Some are quick and cheap. Some are slow and
careful. Some are outside contractors.

Someone has to decide who gets which job. If every product picked its own worker, nobody could say
afterwards who did what, or why.

```panel big
**engine is the dispatch office.** One script, `arc-run.mjs`, does the whole routine for every job:

- **The job description** (a process). One file that says what the job is, which tools the worker may touch, and the exact shape the finished answer must have. It never names a worker.
- **The staffing rota** (`engine/router.yaml`). One hand-edited file that says which grade of worker handles which kind of job. It changes only when a person edits it and the change is reviewed.
- **The phone lines** (drivers). The code that can actually reach one kind of worker. Each worker has its own line.
- **The logbook** (the spine). After every run, one line goes in: who did it, which decision picked them, and what it cost. Lines are added and never rewritten.

The office never does the work itself. It sends, checks, and records.
```

### Why this needs to be a product at all

If one worker did everything, you would not need an office. arc wants many workers, and that brings
three quiet problems:

| What you lose | What it looks like when it bites | engine's answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Who did the work** | A bad call turns up weeks later and nobody can say which model made it. | Every run writes a logbook line naming the worker and whose decision chose them. |
| **Who changed the rota** | Someone flips a setting and a cheap job quietly starts running on the expensive worker. | The rota lives in one file, changed only by a reviewed edit, never during a run. |
| **Whether the answer is real** | A worker hands back something neat, well-shaped and wrong. | The answer is checked against the job's own description before anything accepts it. |

> The third row does a second job. When an answer fails, engine can tell whether the job description
> was broken or the worker was too weak for the seat, so it never blames a worker for a bad brief.

## arc words → normal words

```lede
Ten pieces of arc jargon. Each is an ordinary office thing wearing a technical name.
```

```rosetta
process | the job description | one file: the tools allowed and the shape of a valid answer
`engine/router.yaml` | the staffing rota | which grade of worker handles which kind of job
tier | the pay grade | how hard the work is, never a brand name
driver | the phone line | the code that reaches one worker
receipt / the spine | one line in the logbook | who ran, which model, how long, what it cost
hire row | the contractor's contract | a rota row pointing at an outside runtime, with extra terms
`review_by` | the contract end date | past it, the row is refused, not quietly renewed
trial | a one-off audition | try a named worker for one run, without touching the rota
`model_source` | whose decision picked the worker | so a logbook line is never mistaken for a rota decision
data boundary | the "not for outsiders" check | internal-only papers never go to an outside worker
```

## How a job flows

```lede
Several doors check the job before any money is spent. After the worker answers, the answer is checked
too, and only then is the logbook written.
```

```flow
source: arc-run --process <name>
box: ① Sensible? | real job, real folder, budget left
box: ② Look up the rota | grade, phone line, worker
box: ③ Contract and boundary | terms, then the papers
box*: ④ Send, check, log | the money starts here
labels: routed, cleared, answered
out: bad request | stops, nothing spent
out: unknown job | stops, names the rota file
out: internal-only | refused, exit 5
out+: run.completed | one line in the logbook
divider: 3 | free to refuse | costs money
note: A refusal before the divider costs nothing. A run after it always leaves a logbook line.
caption: Figure 1 — one arc-run. | The dashed red line is where the office starts spending.
```

## The stages, one by one

```lede
Each stage is written twice: first what it does in ordinary words, then what actually happens.
```

```steps
t: Check the paperwork before anyone starts
plain: Is this a real job, is the destination a real folder, is there any budget left? All of it is checked before a single worker is contacted, because a bad destination found later has already cost money.
d: The guards run first: a known process name, a work folder that exists and is not this repo itself, and a budget that has not already run out.
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/arc-run.mjs`

t: Look up who does this kind of job
plain: The job's name is found in the rota. The rota row says which grade, which phone line, and sometimes which exact worker. A job the rota has never heard of stops right there and names the file to fix.
d: An unknown class exits non-zero naming the class and `engine/router.yaml`, because the fix is always to edit that file and never to guess.
f: `engine/router.yaml`

t: If the worker is a contractor, read the contract
plain: A contractor's row carries extra terms, checked when the rota is loaded and not when the row is used. Past the end date, the job is refused.
d: The four terms are `cap`, `hosted`, `judge` and `review_by`. An expired row refuses the dispatch rather than being silently renewed or silently switched off.
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/router-row.mjs` · ADR-0216

t: Check the papers may leave the building
plain: The job's input is scanned for an internal-only marker before any worker exists. If it carries one, it is refused at the door, so the paper never reaches the outside worker.
d: The check runs above the driver, at arc-run, which is why a refusal happens before a driver process is even spawned.
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/data-boundary.mjs` · ADR-0219

t: Send the job out
plain: The driver runs on its own, and the worker is handed to it down exactly one path. No stray setting on the machine can swap the worker without anyone reviewing it.
d: arc-run sets `ARC_DRIVER_MODEL` on the driver's environment. A trial run uses `--trial-model` for that one run only and writes nothing to the rota (ADR-0220).
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/drivers/common.mjs`

t: Check the finished work, and say whose fault a failure is
plain: The answer must match the shape the job description asked for. If it does not, the same grade gets one more try. If it fails again, the job description's own worked examples are checked. If those fail too, the brief was broken and no worker is blamed.
d: Escalation never changes a grade during a run. After the one retry, engine raises an `approval.requested` proposal and stops, and a person edits the rota in a reviewed diff (ADR-0069).
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/arc-run.mjs` · `.claude/scripts/engine/schema-subset.mjs`

t: Write it in the logbook
plain: One line: who did it, which decision picked them, how long it took, what it cost. A cost that was never reported stays blank. It is never guessed and never set to zero.
d: A `run.completed` receipt, on failure paths as well as on success.
f: `.claude/scripts/engine/arc-run.mjs`
```

# The bigger loop

## A story, from one job to the next

```lede
The story below is an illustration of how a run goes, not a record of a real one.
```

Say the drafting job `commit-msg-draft` is sent out.

1. The office finds it in the rota, sees the grade and the phone line, and sends it out.
2. The worker answers, but leaves out a required field. That is a failure of shape.
3. The office retries once on the same grade. Same problem.
4. Now it checks the job's own worked examples. They pass, so the brief is fine, and the fault is the worker's.
5. The office does not quietly move the job to a stronger worker. It raises a proposal for a person and stops.
6. A person reads the proposal, edits the rota in a reviewed change, and the next run uses the new row.
7. The logbook shows both runs, so the change can be traced to the failure that caused it.

## What engine also owns

- **The attack pass.** `/arc-attack` sends two fresh attackers at a finished change, one on its logic and one on its edges. Each gets only the diff and no tools, which is what keeps it fresh (ADR-0226). It reports and never fixes.
- **Generated commands.** `/arc-commit`, `/arc-review` and `/arc-kickoff` are compiled from job descriptions by `arc-compile.mjs`. A hand edit to one is deleted on the next compile. Change the job description instead.
- **The job list.** Which jobs exist, and which script or command runs them, is in the generated sections of this page, not restated here.

## Where engine sits in arc

- **Underneath the others.** Products that want a model to do a job go through the office, so their runs land in one logbook.
- **The pay grades come from policy.** The rota implements ADR-0069 and decides no "which model where" question of its own.
- **In the face.** engine lives in the room for the machinery that runs the other products. The chips at the top of this page name the room and the ring.

# Meta

## Glossary

```gloss
headless: run by a script with nobody at the keyboard, in contrast to an interactive chat session.
schema: a written description of the exact shape an answer must have, such as which fields exist and what type each is.
append-only: new lines can be added to the end, and old lines are never edited or removed.
diff: the list of exactly what changed between two versions of the files.
```
